overview:
Adinath Neminath Upadhye (1906–1975) was one of the most important twentieth‑century scholars of Prakrit, Jainology, and classical Indian literature. Born in Sadalga in the Belgaum district (present‑day Karnataka) into a traditional Jain priestly (Upadhyaya) family, he received his early education in Kannada at home and in local schools before moving on to formal higher studies. He completed his secondary education at Gilginchi Artal High School, Belgaum, and then earned a Bachelor of Arts with honours from Bombay University, specializing in Sanskrit and Prakrit. For postgraduate work he joined the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Poona, where he studied under major Indological figures such as S. K. Belvalkar and V. S. Sukthankar, whose emphasis on rigorous textual criticism and careful editing deeply shaped his scholarly method.

In 1930, Upadhye completed his Master of Arts in Sanskrit and Prakrit, again from Bombay University, and in the same year began his long teaching career as Lecturer in Ardhamāgadhī/Prakrit at Rajaram College, Kolhapur. He was confirmed as Professor in 1933 and served there for roughly three decades. In 1939 he received the D.Litt. degree from Bombay University, marking formal recognition of his already substantial contributions to Prakrit and Jain studies. Between 1939 and the early 1940s he worked as a Springer Research Scholar, continuing intensive research and editorial projects. After retiring from Rajaram College in 1962, he was appointed Professor Emeritus at Shivaji University (Kolhapur), where he also served as Dean of the Arts Faculty and helped lay the institutional foundations of the new university.

In the later phase of his career, Upadhye became the founding Professor of Jainology and Prakrit at Mysore University, holding the chair in the early 1970s. He also participated in national and international scholarly networks: he presided over sections on Prakrit, Pali, Jainism, and Buddhism at the All‑India Oriental Conference, served as General President of the same conference in 1966, and was elected President of the 46th Kannada Sāhitya Sammelana held at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa in 1967. As a delegate of the Government of India he attended international congresses of Orientalists and conferences on religion and peace in Canberra, Paris, Leuven, and other centres, reflecting the global recognition of his expertise.

Upadhye’s scholarly output was vast and technically sophisticated. By the mid‑1950s bibliographies already listed dozens of books, critical editions, and nearly a hundred research papers; by the time of his death the total had grown substantially. His work spans Prakrit, Sanskrit, and Kannada, and includes critical editions of major Jain scriptures and narrative texts, studies of Prakrit language and literature, and essays on the history of Indian and specifically Jain literary traditions. Among his most celebrated achievements is his co‑editing, with Hiralal Jain, of the monumental multi‑volume edition of the Digambara Jain scripture "Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama" together with its extensive commentary "Dhavalā"—a project that required mastery of Prakrit, Sanskrit, textual criticism, and doctrinal detail. He also produced editions and studies of works such as "Nyāyāvatāra", "Pañcasuttaṃ", "Bṛhatkathākośa", "Varāhacarita", "Ātmanuśāsana", and several texts of Ācārya Kundakunda and other Jain authors.

In Kannada, Upadhye contributed both original scholarship and critical engagement with classical literature. His book "Pāli and Prakrit" and articles on texts like "Vaḍḍārādhane" and "Dharmaparīkṣe" helped situate Jain and Prakrit materials within the broader history of Kannada prose and poetry. He wrote on the poet Ranna, on the background of early Jain‑Kannada narrative, and on the role of Prakrit in the formation of Jain religious literature. His linguistic range was notable: in addition to his mother tongue Kannada, he had working knowledge of Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, German, and French, which enabled him to interact with both Indian and European scholarship.

Within Jain studies, Upadhye is remembered not only for the quantity of his publications but for their methodological rigor. He consistently emphasized the importance of establishing reliable critical texts as the foundation for doctrinal, philosophical, and literary interpretation. His editions typically include detailed introductions, philological notes, and discussions of manuscript traditions. This approach made his work central to later research on Jain karma theory, cosmology, narrative literature, and Prakrit philology. Many of his editions and studies remain standard references in Digambara Jain scholarship and in academic Prakritology.

Dr. A. N. Upadhye passed away in 1975, shortly after retiring from his post at Mysore University. Colleagues and students described his death as a major loss for Prakrit studies, sometimes saying that "Prakritology had become orphaned" without his guiding presence. His legacy continues through the texts he edited, the students he trained, and the institutional structures he helped build for the academic study of Jainism and Prakrit. For contemporary Jain studies, he stands as a key figure in the transition from traditional pandit scholarship to modern, critically grounded Indology, while remaining deeply rooted in Jain religious and linguistic traditions.

primary_sources.title: Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama with Dhavalā commentary (selected verse)
primary_sources.author: Attributed to Ācārya Puṣpadanta and Bhūtabali; commentary by Ācārya Virasena; critically edited by A. N. Upadhye and Hiralal Jain
primary_sources.translation: Karmas are the causes of bondage for the soul; these bondages, each yielding its own specific result.
primary_sources.notes: The multi‑volume critical edition of the Digambara Jain scripture "Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama" with the "Dhavalā" commentary is one of A. N. Upadhye’s most significant editorial achievements. Working with Hiralal Jain and others, he collated manuscripts, standardized readings, and provided scholarly apparatus that made this foundational karma‑doctrine text accessible to modern researchers. The sample verse illustrates the central Jain idea that karmic influx and bondage condition the soul’s experience and spiritual progress.

primary_sources.title: Pañcasuttaṃ (Ardhamāgadhī Jain text, critical edition)
primary_sources.author: Traditional Jain authorship; critical edition by A. N. Upadhye
primary_sources.original_text:
णमो अरिहंताणं, णमो सिद्धाणं,
णमो आयरियाणं, णमो उवज्झायाणं,
णमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ṇamo arihaṃtāṇaṃ, ṇamo siddhāṇaṃ,
ṇamo āyariyāṇaṃ, ṇamo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ,
ṇamo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ
primary_sources.translation:
Obeisance to the Arhats, obeisance to the Siddhas,
obeisance to the Ācāryas, obeisance to the Upādhyāyas,
obeisance to all Sādhus in the world.
primary_sources.notes: Upadhye’s early critical edition of "Pañcasuttaṃ" exemplifies his work on Prakrit devotional and doctrinal texts. The passage is a well‑known Jain prayer formula, closely related to the Namokāra mantra, and shows the liturgical context of many texts he edited. His edition provided a reliable Ardhamāgadhī text, with introduction and notes, for both traditional and academic readers.

primary_sources.title: Nyāyāvatāra (Jain philosophical text)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Siddhasena Divākara; edited and studied by A. N. Upadhye
primary_sources.translation: Means of valid knowledge are said to be three: perception, inference, and scripture.
primary_sources.notes: Upadhye’s work on "Nyāyāvatāra" reflects his interest in Jain epistemology and logic. By preparing a critical text and engaging with its philosophical content, he helped situate Jain theories of knowledge within broader Indian philosophical debates. The verse cited summarizes a key Jain position on pramāṇas (valid means of knowledge).

primary_sources.title: Vaḍḍārādhane (Old Kannada Jain prose work, discussed by Upadhye)
primary_sources.author: Śivakōṭi Ācārya (traditional attribution); critically studied by A. N. Upadhye
primary_sources.original_text: इह लोकदल् परलोकदल् पवित्रवागि जीवन् नडेदुवन् धर्मवु।
primary_sources.transliteration: iha lokadal paralokadal pavitravāgi jīvan naḍeduvaṃ dharmavu
primary_sources.translation: Dharma is the way of living in this world and the next in a pure manner.
primary_sources.notes: Although Vaḍḍārādhane is a Kannada text rather than Prakrit or Sanskrit, Upadhye’s articles on it are central to his contribution to Jain‑Kannada literary history. He analyzed its language, narrative structure, and religious themes, showing how Jain narrative and ethical ideas were expressed in early Kannada prose. The sentence here is representative rather than a fixed canonical line, illustrating the ethical orientation of the work.

misconceptions.myth: A. N. Upadhye was primarily a Kannada literary figure and only secondarily a Jain or Prakrit scholar.
misconceptions.reality: While Upadhye made important contributions to Kannada literary history and wrote in Kannada, his central and defining work was in Prakrit and Jainology. He is widely recognized as one of the foremost twentieth‑century scholars of Prakrit language and Jain scriptures, with major critical editions of Digambara canonical and commentarial texts, as well as extensive research on Jain philosophy and literature.

misconceptions.myth: Upadhye’s editions are simply traditional reproductions of Jain texts without modern critical method.
misconceptions.reality: Upadhye was trained in modern Indological textual criticism at institutions such as the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute and worked under scholars who emphasized rigorous manuscript collation and critical editing. His editions of texts like "Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama" and "Pañcasuttaṃ" apply these methods, providing carefully established texts, introductions, and notes. They are considered foundational scholarly resources rather than uncritical reproductions.

misconceptions.myth: Because he came from a priestly Jain family, Upadhye’s work is purely sectarian and not of interest to academic study.
misconceptions.reality: Upadhye’s background gave him deep familiarity with Jain tradition, but his training and career were firmly within academic institutions, and his work is widely cited in university‑based Jain studies and Indology. His scholarship bridges traditional learning and modern academic standards, making his editions and studies valuable to both religious communities and secular researchers.

misconceptions.myth: Upadhye focused only on Digambara texts and ignored Śvetāmbara and broader Indian literature.
misconceptions.reality: Although many of his major editorial projects concern Digambara scriptures and commentaries, Upadhye’s range includes Prakrit and Sanskrit works relevant across Jain sects, as well as studies of Pali, Apabhraṃśa, and Kannada literature. He engaged with the wider history of Indian literature and philosophy, and his linguistic competence allowed him to work across sectarian and regional boundaries.
